project.name: arbitrage-agents

nodes.name: crypto-market-normalizer.ts
nodes.summary: Normalizes raw venue market snapshots into structured crypto market descriptors by parsing assets, price thresholds, operators, deadlines, resolution sources, and ambiguity flags.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses regex-driven TypeScript parsing helpers to convert heterogeneous prediction-market text into deterministic domain fields.

nodes.summary: Provides the scanner persistence port plus an in-memory implementation that records scan runs, snapshots, normalized markets, candidate pairs, and opportunities for tests or local runs.

nodes.name: postgres-scanner-repository.ts

nodes.languageNotes: SQL statements are embedded directly in repository methods and use JSONB payloads for flexible domain data.

nodes.name: read-only-scanner.ts

nodes.name: scanner-result.ts

nodes.name: static-venue-client.ts

nodes.name: venue-market.ts

nodes.name: normalizer.test.ts

nodes.name: scanner.test.ts
nodes.summary: Tests that the read-only scanner persists scan runs, snapshots, normalized markets, candidate pairs, and opportunities when driven by static venue clients.

nodes.name: CryptoMarketNormalizer
nodes.summary: Transforms a venue market snapshot into a normalized crypto market by delegating extraction of semantic fields to focused parsing helpers.

nodes.name: parseThreshold
nodes.summary: Extracts a numeric price threshold from explicit dollar patterns or comparative phrases while avoiding unrelated text when possible.

nodes.name: parseDeadline
nodes.summary: Parses either ISO timestamps or January date phrases into UTC ISO deadline strings for normalized markets.

nodes.name: ambiguityFlagsFor
nodes.summary: Builds normalization ambiguity flags for missing asset, threshold, operator, resolution source, or deadline fields.

nodes.name: InMemoryScannerRepository
nodes.summary: Stores scanner artifacts in arrays while implementing the shared scanner repository contract for tests and lightweight local execution.

nodes.name: PostgresScannerRepository

nodes.name: uuidFromStableKey
nodes.summary: Derives deterministic UUID-shaped identifiers from stable domain keys for database rows that originate outside PostgreSQL.

nodes.name: ReadOnlyScanner

nodes.name: KalshiPublicVenueClient

nodes.name: PolymarketPublicVenueClient

nodes.name: StaticVenueClient

nodes.name: snapshot

nodes.name: market

tour.title: Product Scope
tour.description: Start with the product requirements and scope documents to understand why this project exists before reading runtime code. Together they define the scanner as a read-only cross-venue prediction-market arbitrage intelligence system focused first on Kalshi and Polymarket, with explicit non-goals such as autonomous trading and deferred IBKR integration. This framing explains why the rest of the architecture emphasizes normalization, persistence, observability, and API read models rather than order execution.

tour.title: Architecture Decisions
tour.description: The architecture decision record turns the product scope into implementation boundaries. It explains the choice of a DDD-inspired NestJS modular monolith with separate API and worker runtimes, PostgreSQL persistence, Drizzle migrations, and stateless persisted LLM calls. Read this after the PRD so the later module split feels intentional rather than accidental.
tour.languageLesson: ADR documents capture architectural decisions with context and rejected alternatives, which helps newcomers distinguish deliberate constraints from incidental implementation details.

tour.title: Runtime Entry Points
tour.description: The project has two runtime paths: the API process serves read-only HTTP views, while the worker process performs one scanner pass and exits. The API and worker application modules keep each process focused by composing only the configuration and context modules it needs. This split is the backbone for understanding how scanner writes and API reads stay decoupled while sharing the same database model.
tour.languageLesson: NestJS modules are composition roots: they declare which providers and controllers are available for a particular application context.

tour.title: Configuration Backbone
tour.description: Configuration is loaded once from the environment, validated, normalized, and exposed through a global NestJS provider. This matters because both the API and worker need consistent database, port, venue, telemetry, and sampling settings without duplicating parsing logic. The package manifest and environment template show how those settings connect to the project scripts and deployment surface.
tour.languageLesson: Zod-style configuration validation turns untyped environment variables into a typed runtime contract, catching invalid ports or malformed settings during startup instead of later in the request path.

tour.title: API Read Model
tour.description: After the API bootstrap, the read-model layer exposes scanner state through health, market, opportunity, and scan-run controllers. Controllers stay thin by delegating to read services and repository contracts, while the PostgreSQL adapter translates stored rows into response-oriented models. This is the consumer-facing side of the system: it never scans markets itself, it only reads the artifacts produced by the worker.

tour.title: Venue Contracts
tour.description: The scanner talks to venues through a shared domain contract rather than hard-coding Kalshi or Polymarket inside the pipeline. Public HTTP clients adapt each venue API into that common snapshot shape, while the static client supplies deterministic data for offline runs and tests. This adapter boundary is what lets the domain pipeline compare markets without caring where the raw payload came from.
tour.languageLesson: The adapter pattern keeps external API differences at the edge: venue-specific payloads are converted once into internal contracts that the rest of the code can treat uniformly.

tour.title: Domain Vocabulary
tour.description: Before following the scanner pipeline, learn the shared market and opportunity types that have the highest fan-in in the graph. Normalized markets give every venue listing a comparable identity, candidate pairs connect possible cross-venue matches, and opportunities represent detected arbitrage with risk and book details. These types form the vocabulary used by matching, scanning, persistence, and API read models.

tour.title: Matching Intelligence
tour.description: The matching layer converts messy venue text into structured comparable markets, generates plausible Kalshi-to-Polymarket pairs, and classifies whether those pairs are equivalent enough to evaluate. This is where the project encodes domain judgment: thresholds, deadlines, resolution sources, ambiguity flags, and material mismatch reasons all affect whether a pair should be trusted. It builds directly on the shared vocabulary from the previous step.
tour.languageLesson: Regex-driven normalization is useful at system edges, but the important design move is to immediately convert parsed text into explicit typed fields and ambiguity flags.

tour.title: Opportunity Calculation
tour.description: Once markets are normalized and paired, the arbitrage domain service turns candidate pairs into executable opportunity records. It validates order books, evaluates trade directions, builds legs, and computes net edge after costs such as fees and slippage. This is the core business calculation that makes the scanner more than a market-matching index.

tour.title: Scanner Orchestration
tour.description: The worker runner assembles real infrastructure for one scan cycle, while the read-only scanner coordinates the full pipeline: fetch venues, normalize markets, generate pairs, classify equivalence, calculate opportunities, and persist each artifact. Scanner result types capture lifecycle status and metrics so failures can be reported without placing trades. This step connects the domain services from earlier steps into the worker execution path introduced at the beginning.

tour.title: Persistence Model
tour.description: Persistence is shared by the writer-side scanner repository and the reader-side API repositories. The Drizzle schema and SQL migration define scan runs, raw venue snapshots, normalized markets, candidate pairs, LLM evaluations, order books, opportunities, and alerts, giving every pipeline artifact a durable home. The PostgreSQL scanner repository then writes stable domain-derived records into those tables for the API to read later.
tour.languageLesson: Drizzle migrations are the ordered database history, while the TypeScript schema gives application code a typed representation of the same tables.

tour.title: LLM Observability Tests
tour.description: The LLM and observability layer adds optional judgment and safety around the deterministic scanner. Persisted LLM evaluation records use deterministic hashing and validation to cache successful responses, while redaction and observability services prevent secrets from leaking into captured events. The Vitest suite anchors the architecture by testing configuration, matching, arbitrage, scanner persistence, LLM caching, and observability behavior.
tour.languageLesson: Vitest specs here work as executable architecture documentation: they show the intended behavior of domain services, adapters, repositories, and safety boundaries.
